Tabs (A):
- Pros: Allow individual developers to set their own preferred indentation width in their editor (accessibility benefit for visual preference); smaller file size (marginally); single keystroke per indent level.
- Cons: Can cause misalignment when mixed with spaces (e.g., in comments, ASCII diagrams, or alignment of code after the indent level) if editor settings differ across contributors; some diff/blame tools render tabs inconsistently; alignment of wrapped lines or trailing content after an indent can look inconsistent across editors.

Spaces (B):
- Pros: Renders identically in every editor, terminal, diff viewer, and code review tool, since there's no dependency on tab-width settings; enables precise alignment (e.g., multi-line function arguments) that stays visually consistent everywhere; is the more common default in many modern style guides and linters (e.g., PEP 8 for Python, Google style guides, Prettier defaults) for exactly this reason.
- Cons: Slightly more keystrokes unless the editor auto-inserts space blocks on Tab press; marginally larger file size; no per-developer customization of visual indent width.

In terms of objective, verifiable properties, spaces produce more deterministic, tool-agnostic results across environments, which is likely why they've become the more common default in many widely-adopted style guides. Tabs offer a legitimate accessibility/customization advantage but require stricter tooling discipline (e.g., .editorconfig, linters) to avoid inconsistency in a multi-contributor codebase.
